newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Dalai Lama meeting won't hurt China ties-Canberra.
newsitem.headline: Dalai Lama meeting won't hurt China ties-Canberra.

text.p: Australia's deputy prime minister on Wednesday defended Prime Minister John Howard's decision to meet Tibet's exiled spiritual leader the Dalai Lama, saying he was confident it would not upset ties with China.

"I believe that the size, the very volume of the business relationship, the political relationship is so large today that no one circumstance should be allowed to derail (relations)," Tim Fischer told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.

Beijing, which regards the Buddhist god-king as a pro-independence campaigner bent on splitting China, threatened trade retaliation on Tuesday after Howard announced he would meet the Dalai Lama on Thursday.
Foreign ministry spokesman Shen Guofang said Canberra was meddling in China's internal affairs and warned the meeting "would cast a shadow over Sino-Australian relations".
"This shadow will of course affect affect Sino-Australian political ties. It is unavoidable that it will also affect Sino-Australian trade ties," he told reporters.
Fischer, urging Beijing not to penalise Australian business, said he hoped the row would not undermine a push for closer bilateral relations.
"...These are matters which I hope will not derail the great common purpose that exists in building our business and diplomatic links between Australia and China," Fischer said.
Fischer stressed Howard was meeting the Dalai Lama as a spiritual leader and that the talks were unofficial.
"Mr Howard will be meeting the Dalai Lama only in that role and a long way from his official prime ministerial office at parliament house in Canberra," he said.
But the meeting will be held at Howard's Sydney office, where he conducts most of his official business when parliament is not sitting. Parliament is in recess this week.

The Dalai Lama, exiled since an abortive 1959 uprising against Chinese rule in his Himalayan homeland, has urged Howard to press Beijing to open negotiations on autonomy for the vast but sparsely-populated region.
Relations between Beijing and Canberra have soured recently over a range of diplomatic and security issues, including a proposal to sell Australian uranium to Taiwan.
